patient.name: Chloe Adeyemi-Hart
patient.setting: GP surgery, then the breast surgical unit
patient.complaint: Painful, red left breast and fever, 4 weeks after giving birth
background: First baby, born 4 weeks ago, exclusively breastfed

diagnosis.exam: Expect a breastfeeding woman with a red, tender breast and fever; the question is mastitis vs abscess, decided by a **fluctuant** lump, or 'most likely finding on examination'.

points: Left nipple **cracked** and sore for two weeks.
Baby skipped feeds on the left: it hurt too much.
Now: hot, **red, tender** left breast and a **burning** pain.
Feels shivery and achy, like flu.

steps.lead: Chloe ticks almost every box: **childbearing age**, breastfeeding, a **cracked nipple**, **milk stasis** from skipped feeds, and she smokes.
Her swelling, tenderness, redness, burning, fever and **flu-like** aches are the textbook presentation.

points: Examination: wedge-shaped red, warm area, upper outer left breast.
Tender and firm, but **no discrete lump**, nothing fluctuant.
No axillary mass; right breast normal.

steps.lead: No collection is felt, so this is **lactational mastitis**, most likely from **Staphylococcus aureus**.

steps.q: Chloe has a red, tender wedge and fever, but no lump. What is the diagnosis?
steps.r: Inflamed breast tissue with **no fluctuant mass** in a breastfeeding woman is mastitis. An abscess needs a fluctuant lump.

points: Day 5: she returns. Pain worse despite feeding and expressing.
Now a **3 cm hot, tender lump** under the red skin.
It is **fluctuant**: it feels like a fluid-filled balloon.

steps.lead: The new **fluctuant** swelling is the switch from mastitis to **breast abscess**.

visual.title: Chloe's course at home
visual.caption: Fever that will not settle despite good milk removal: look for an abscess.

steps.title: Mastitis vs abscess vs other lumps
head: Feature
Mastitis
Breast abscess
Inflammatory cancer

steps.lead: Chloe's pulse is rising with a fever. Check for **sepsis** (NEWS2, lactate) before you call it a simple local infection.

steps.text: A red breast in a woman who is **not** breastfeeding and has no fever is not mastitis until proven otherwise: think **inflammatory breast cancer**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'most appropriate investigation' for a fluctuant lump in a lactating breast: **breast ultrasound**. Mastitis alone needs none.

steps.q: Chloe now has a fluctuant lump. Which investigation confirms an abscess?
steps.r: **Ultrasound** is gold standard for a suspected abscess and can guide aspiration at the same time.

steps.lead: Her first visit needed **no tests**: mastitis is clinical. Day 5's fluctuant lump needs an **ultrasound**.

visual.title: Ultrasound: collection size
visual.label: Chloe 3.2 cm
visual.caption: A hypoechoic, walled-off collection confirms the abscess. Size and loculation guide aspiration versus drainage.

steps.title: Bloods on the breast unit
steps.text: Raised inflammatory markers, normal lactate: infected but not septic shock.
Send the aspirated **pus** and a **breast milk sample** for culture and sensitivities: it confirms **S. aureus** and catches MRSA.
Mammogram is not the test for a lactating breast abscess: dense breast tissue and pain make it useless here.

management.exam: Expect 'next step in management': continue breastfeeding for mastitis, flucloxacillin when triggers are met, and surgical drainage for an abscess.

steps.title: Mastitis to abscess pathway
nodes: No better after 12–24 h, cracked nipple or unwell → flucloxacillin 10 days
Abscess → surgeons: aspiration or incision and drainage + antibiotics
steps.caption: Each step up needs a trigger: time, a fissure, systemic illness, or a lump.

steps.q: On day 1 Chloe asks whether she should stop breastfeeding. What do you advise?
o: Stop feeding from the left breast
Switch to formula until antibiotics finish
steps.r: **Continued milk removal** is first-line: it drains the blocked duct and is safe for the baby.

steps.lead: Day 1 plan for Chloe: **keep feeding** from both sides, express what is left, and take **paracetamol or ibuprofen**.

visual.title: Hours of effective milk removal without improvement
visual.label: Chloe 24 h
visual.caption: Chloe also has a cracked nipple (an infected fissure), another reason to start antibiotics.

steps.lead: Chloe was no better after 24 hours and had a fissure, so she got **flucloxacillin for 10 days**. Penicillin allergy would mean **clarithromycin**.

steps.q: Day 5: ultrasound shows a 3.2 cm collection. What is the next step?
o: Stop breastfeeding and review in 1 week
steps.r: A walled-off abscess will not resolve with antibiotics alone. It needs **urgent surgical drainage**.

steps.lead: Chloe goes to the **general surgeons** for **ultrasound-guided aspiration** (or incision and drainage), staying on flucloxacillin.

visual.title: After drainage
visual.caption: Once the pus is out, markers fall fast.

steps.text: Avoid **aspirin** for pain while breastfeeding: it passes into milk and risks **Reye's syndrome** in the baby.
Exam rule: no lump → keep feeding (antibiotics only if triggers); **fluctuant lump → drainage**. Co-amoxiclav is a distractor.

science.exam: Expect applied questions on the organism (**S. aureus**), why milk stasis and cracked nipples cause infection, or why abscesses need drainage.

steps.title: From blocked duct to abscess
nodes: Cracked nipple lets in S. aureus
Unresolved: pus walls off into an abscess

steps.lead: Chloe's skipped left-sided feeds left milk sitting in the ducts: a **nidus** for bacteria to grow.
Her **cracked nipple** was the **portal of entry** for S. aureus from the baby's mouth and her skin.
By day 5 the infection had **walled off**. Antibiotics cannot penetrate a pus cavity well, hence drainage.
Chloe keeps feeding because emptying the breast **clears the infected duct**, and the milk does not harm her son.

steps.q: Why did flucloxacillin alone fail to cure Chloe by day 5?
o: A walled-off pus collection is poorly penetrated by antibiotics
S. aureus is always resistant to flucloxacillin
steps.r: Abscesses are **avascular, walled-off** cavities: antibiotics struggle to reach the bacteria, so pus must be drained.

steps.text: **Flucloxacillin** is a penicillinase-resistant penicillin: it survives the beta-lactamase most S. aureus produce.

mcq.q: Most common organism in lactational mastitis?
mcq.r: **S. aureus** causes both mastitis and breast abscess.

mcq.q: Which feature distinguishes a breast abscess from mastitis?
mcq.r: Redness, fever and tenderness occur in both; a **fluctuant** lump means pus.

mcq.q: Which is a risk factor for mastitis?
mcq.r: Cracked nipples, milk stasis, breastfeeding, smoking and childbearing age.

mcq.q: Which complication makes mastitis an emergency?
mcq.r: Systemic illness or spreading infection raises concern for **sepsis**.

mcq.q: Gold-standard investigation for suspected breast abscess?
mcq.r: **Ultrasound** confirms the collection and guides aspiration.

mcq.q: Penicillin-allergic woman with mastitis needs antibiotics. Which?
mcq.r: **Clarithromycin** is the alternative in penicillin allergy.

mcq.q: Why do cracked nipples increase infection risk?
mcq.r: They let **S. aureus** from infant oral flora into breast tissue.

technique.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 4 day history of pain in her left breast. She is breastfeeding her 5 week old daughter. She had antibiotics from her GP 3 days ago but feels worse. There is a tender, erythematous 3 cm lump in the upper outer quadrant that is fluctuant. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis. In a breastfeeding woman with a red breast, the decision is mastitis vs abscess.

clues: antibiotics from her GP 3 days ago but feels worse
steps.x: Lactation, partly treated infection, fever, and a fluctuant tender lump.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mastitis that has failed treatment and now has a fluctuant lump: **breast abscess**.

elim: Duct ectasia is perimenopausal with nipple discharge and retraction, not an acute febrile lump.
A fibroadenoma is a non-tender, mobile, firm lump with no fever.
Inflammatory cancer is not fluctuant or febrile and occurs outside lactation.
Mastitis has no discrete **fluctuant** mass.

steps.x: **A. Breast abscess.** Rule: fluctuant lump in a breastfeeding woman = abscess.

technique.stem: A 31 year old woman who is breastfeeding has a painful, red right breast. She has been taking flucloxacillin for 4 days. On examination there is a 2 cm tender, fluctuant swelling beneath the areola. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: It asks for the diagnostic test, so first name the suspected diagnosis.
A fluctuant swelling on antibiotics means a suspected abscess.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Suspected abscess: **breast ultrasound** (gold standard, can guide aspiration).

elim: Useful if septic, but they do not show a collection.
Biopsy is for a suspected tumour, not an infected collection.
Mammography is poor in the dense, painful lactating breast.
MRI is not first-line and adds delay; ultrasound answers the question.

steps.x: **B. Breast ultrasound.** Rule: mastitis is clinical; suspected abscess gets ultrasound.

technique.stem: A 24 year old woman has had pain and redness in her left breast for 1 day. She is breastfeeding her 6 week old son. There is a tender, red, wedge-shaped area in the lower outer quadrant. No mass is palpable and her nipples are intact. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Stop breastfeeding and express to discard

steps.x: It asks for initial management. Decide mastitis or abscess, then check the antibiotic triggers.
Short history, no mass, no fissure, systemically well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Uncomplicated mastitis: **keep feeding/expressing** plus paracetamol or ibuprofen.

elim: Antibiotics wait until no improvement after 12–24 h of milk removal, a fissure or systemic illness.
There is no mass, so nothing to drain.
Milk is safe for the baby; stopping worsens stasis.
Mastitis is clinical; ultrasound is for a suspected abscess.

steps.x: **A. Continue breastfeeding and simple analgesia.** Rule: no triggers, no antibiotics yet.

technique.stem: A 30 year old woman has a hot, swollen, tender right breast 3 weeks after delivery. She has painful cracked nipples and her baby feeds poorly from the right side. Her temperature is 38.2°C. A milk culture is sent.
technique.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?

steps.x: It asks for the organism. Recognise the condition first, then recall its commonest bug.

clues: feeds poorly from the right side
steps.x: Puerperal mastitis with a skin portal of entry and milk stasis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Commonest organism in mastitis and abscess: **S. aureus**.

elim: Candida causes nipple pain and itching, not a febrile inflamed breast.
E. coli is a gut and urinary organism, not a breast skin coloniser.
Possible but much less common than S. aureus.
Pseudomonas is hospital and burns-associated, not lactational mastitis.

steps.x: **E. Staphylococcus aureus.** Rule: think S. aureus, so flucloxacillin.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 2 day history of pain in her right breast and feeling shivery. She is breastfeeding her 3 week old son. There is a hot, red, tender wedge-shaped area in the upper outer quadrant. No mass is felt. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A febrile, red, tender wedge with no mass in a breastfeeding woman is mastitis; abscess needs a fluctuant lump.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely diagnosis?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Lactation, inflamed wedge, fever, no lump.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Inflamed breast without a collection: **mastitis**.

elim: No **fluctuant mass** is felt.
Fat necrosis follows trauma and gives a firm lump, not fever.
Cyclical, premenstrual lumpiness, not an acute febrile red breast.
Occurs outside lactation, without fever, with peau d'orange.

steps.x: **E. Lactational mastitis.** No lump = mastitis.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman has had 3 days of pain in her left breast and malaise. She is breastfeeding. Her symptoms have not improved despite effective milk removal and 48 hours of oral antibiotics. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 102 bpm, BP 120/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the left breast?
o: A hard, craggy, fixed mass with skin tethering
A non-tender, firm, smooth, mobile mass
A pea-sized, tender lump under the areola
Bloody nipple discharge from a single duct
practice.e: Mastitis not settling on milk removal and antibiotics suggests an abscess, whose signature sign is a fluctuant, tender, red mass.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely finding on examination of the left breast?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: not improved despite effective milk removal
steps.x: Failed treatment of mastitis with persistent fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Progression to **abscess**: expect a tender, red, **fluctuant** mass.

elim: That describes carcinoma, not a febrile lactational infection.
That is a fibroadenoma.
That fits an intraductal papilloma or small cyst, not a febrile abscess.
Single-duct bloody discharge suggests intraductal papilloma.

steps.x: **D. A tender, erythematous, fluctuant mass.** Failed mastitis treatment → abscess → fluctuant.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman who is breastfeeding has a 4 day history of a painful lump in her right breast. She has a cracked right nipple. There is a 4 cm red, warm, fluctuant swelling at 10 o'clock. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 122/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A hot, fluctuant swelling with fever in a breastfeeding woman is a breast abscess; a galactocele is painless and afebrile.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely diagnosis?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Lactation, portal of entry, fever, fluctuant hot lump.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Breast abscess**.

elim: Cysts are smooth and not hot, red or febrile.
A galactocele is a painless milk-filled cyst without fever or redness.
Mastitis has no fluctuant collection.
A phyllodes tumour grows fast but is painless and afebrile.

steps.x: **A. Breast abscess.** Fluctuant + febrile + breastfeeding = abscess.

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman has a red, painful left breast 2 weeks after delivery. She has painful cracked nipples. Her temperature is 38.1°C. A sample of expressed milk is sent for culture.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: S. aureus is the commonest cause of both lactational mastitis and breast abscess, which is why flucloxacillin is used.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely causative organism?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Puerperal mastitis with a nipple fissure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **S. aureus**.

elim: Anaerobes feature in non-lactational periareolar abscesses in smokers, not puerperal mastitis.
Not a skin or infant oral coloniser.
A respiratory organism.
A respiratory organism, not breast tissue.

steps.x: **D. Staphylococcus aureus.** Treat with flucloxacillin for that reason.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman is breastfeeding her 2 month old son. She attends a postnatal check worried about mastitis. She asks which part of her history most increases her risk. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely risk factor?
practice.e: Milk stasis from infrequent or ineffective feeding is the key risk factor; others include cracked nipples, smoking and childbearing age.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely risk factor?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
A breastfeeding woman; the question is which listed factor raises risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Milk stasis** (alongside cracked nipples and smoking).

elim: Mode of delivery is not a listed risk factor.
Raises cancer risk, not mastitis.
Not a risk factor for mastitis.
Irrelevant to mastitis.

steps.x: **C. Infrequent feeding causing milk stasis.** Stasis is the nidus for infection.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman who is breastfeeding has had a painful, red right breast for 3 days. She now feels very unwell and confused. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.e: Hypotension, tachycardia and confusion with a breast infection mean sepsis, a complication the notes flag as an emergency.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis. Look at the observations before the breast.
Breast infection plus hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnoea and confusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sepsis** from mastitis: an emergency.

elim: She is hypotensive and confused, so this is not a local problem only.
Thyroiditis gives tachycardia but not a red breast, fever and hypotension.
PE gives hypoxia and pleuritic pain, not a red breast with fever.
Simple mastitis does not cause hypotension and confusion.

steps.x: **D. Sepsis secondary to mastitis.** Systemic illness or spread = sepsis until proven otherwise.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman is breastfeeding her 6 week old daughter. She has had a tender, red left breast for 5 days despite oral flucloxacillin. There is a 3 cm tender, fluctuant mass. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 118/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Ultrasound is the gold standard for suspected breast abscess and can guide needle aspiration.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Fluctuant mass on antibiotics: suspected abscess.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Breast ultrasound**.

elim: For suspected malignancy, not abscess.
No role.
Poor in a lactating breast and not the gold standard.
For discharge, not a collection.

steps.x: **A. Breast ultrasound.** Ultrasound can also guide aspiration.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 1 day history of a tender, red area on her right breast. She is breastfeeding her 4 week old son. There is no mass. Her nipples are intact. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: Mastitis is usually diagnosed clinically; ultrasound is for a suspected abscess.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Mild, early mastitis without a lump.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mastitis is a **clinical diagnosis**.

elim: She is systemically well.
Reserved for suspected abscess; there is no mass.
Not indicated in lactational mastitis.
Culture is for failed treatment or recurrence, not routine.

steps.x: **C. Clinical assessment alone.** No lump, no imaging.

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman has right-sided breast pain. She is breastfeeding her 2 month old child and noticed redness this morning. There is a wedge-shaped, tender, red area but no mass. Her nipples are intact. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 84 bpm, BP 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 13 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Continue breastfeeding; antibiotics not yet needed
Stop breastfeeding and start oral antibiotics
practice.e: Uncomplicated mastitis is managed by continuing breastfeeding with analgesia; antibiotics only after 12–24 h without improvement or other triggers.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate next step in management?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Hours-old, no lump, no fissure, well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Keep feeding**, simple analgesia, review if no better in 12–24 h.

elim: She is systemically well.
No mass, so no suspected abscess.
Nothing to drain.
Stopping worsens stasis; no antibiotic trigger yet.

steps.x: **C. Continue breastfeeding; antibiotics not yet needed.** First-line is milk removal.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman has had a painful, red left breast for 2 days. She is breastfeeding and has been expressing effectively, but there is no improvement. She has a cracked left nipple. No mass is felt. She has an anaphylactic penicillin allergy. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Antibiotics are indicated (no improvement, fissure), and clarithromycin replaces flucloxacillin in penicillin allergy.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate management?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Antibiotic triggers met; penicillin allergy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clarithromycin**.

elim: A penicillin: contraindicated.
Contains a penicillin.
First choice normally, but she is penicillin allergic.
No mass to drain.

steps.x: **B. Oral clarithromycin.** Allergy swaps flucloxacillin for clarithromycin.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman has a warm, tender right breast. She is breastfeeding her 3 month old son. There is a 3 cm fluctuant, red, tender lump. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: A breast abscess needs urgent referral to general surgeons for incision and drainage or ultrasound-guided aspiration, with flucloxacillin.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most appropriate management?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Fluctuant lump = abscess.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent surgical drainage** (aspiration or I&D) plus flucloxacillin.

elim: Breastfeeding can continue; it is not the treatment for pus.
Aspirin risks **Reye's syndrome** in the infant.
Flucloxacillin is the antibiotic, and antibiotics alone do not clear an abscess.
A collection needs drainage.

steps.x: **E. Refer to surgeons for drainage.** Abscess = drain it.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has been on flucloxacillin for 5 days for mastitis. She is now febrile with a tender fluctuant lump. Ultrasound shows a 3 cm walled-off collection. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely reason antibiotics alone have failed?
o: Antibiotics penetrate a walled-off pus collection poorly
Flucloxacillin does not cover S. aureus
practice.e: Unresolved inflammation coalesces into a walled-off pus collection that antibiotics alone cannot resolve, so it needs drainage.

steps.x: The lead-in is "Which is the most likely reason antibiotics alone have failed?" Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
An established, walled-off collection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pus coalesces into a **walled-off** cavity antibiotics cannot clear.

elim: Not true.
It is chosen precisely because it covers S. aureus.
The picture is bacterial abscess.
Not true.

steps.x: **A. Antibiotics penetrate a walled-off pus collection poorly.** Hence drainage.

prompts.q: What are mastitis and breast abscess, and what organism causes both?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one word decides the answer: fluctuant.

points.p: Mastitis: infection/inflammation of breast tissue, usually lactational
points.why: Most cases happen in breastfeeding women.

points.p: Abscess: localised pus collection, complication of untreated/inadequate mastitis
points.why: Think abscess when mastitis fails treatment.
This is why flucloxacillin is chosen.

points.why: Fever alone does not mean abscess.

points.why: The key differentiator in the notes.

points.why: Hypotension or confusion makes this an emergency.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: look for a time, a fissure or systemic illness.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: nidus plus portal of entry.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: explain the mechanism, not just the rule.

glossary.Mastitis: Inflammation or infection of breast tissue, most often while breastfeeding.
glossary.Breast abscess: A walled-off collection of pus within the breast, usually after mastitis.
glossary.Lactational: Related to breastfeeding or milk production.
glossary.Puerperal: Occurring in the weeks after childbirth.
glossary.Staphylococcus aureus: Gram-positive coccus in clusters living on skin; the commonest cause of mastitis and abscess.
glossary.MRSA: Meticillin-resistant S. aureus; not killed by flucloxacillin.
glossary.Milk stasis: Milk staying in the ducts because the breast is not emptied well.
glossary.Engorgement: Overfull, swollen, painful breasts from milk building up.
glossary.Nipple fissure: A crack or split in the nipple skin.
glossary.Erythema: Redness of the skin from increased blood flow.
glossary.Fluctuant: A swelling that feels fluid-filled and moves like a water balloon when pressed.
glossary.Nidus: A place where bacteria can settle and multiply.
glossary.Portal of entry: The route by which organisms get into the body.
glossary.Flucloxacillin: A penicillin resistant to staphylococcal beta-lactamase; first choice for S. aureus.
glossary.Clarithromycin: A macrolide antibiotic used when a patient is penicillin allergic.
glossary.Co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid; a broad-spectrum distractor, not first-line for mastitis.
glossary.Beta-lactamase: A bacterial enzyme that breaks down penicillins.
glossary.Incision and drainage: Cutting open an abscess to let the pus out.
glossary.Ultrasound-guided aspiration: Drawing pus out through a needle while watching on ultrasound.
glossary.Hypoechoic: Darker than surrounding tissue on ultrasound; typical of fluid or pus.
glossary.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by the body's response to infection.
glossary.NEWS2: National Early Warning Score 2; a score from vital signs that flags deterioration.
glossary.Lactate: Blood marker of poor tissue perfusion; above 2 mmol/L is a sepsis warning sign.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein; a blood marker that rises with inflammation and infection.
glossary.Inflammatory breast cancer: An aggressive cancer causing a red, swollen breast that mimics infection.
glossary.Peau d'orange: Dimpled breast skin like orange peel, caused by lymphatic blockage from tumour.
glossary.Galactocele: A painless, milk-filled cyst in a breastfeeding woman.
glossary.Reye's syndrome: Rare, serious liver and brain injury in children linked to aspirin.
glossary.Duct ectasia: Widening of the ducts behind the nipple, causing discharge in older women.
glossary.Fibroadenoma: A benign, firm, mobile breast lump in young women.
